paras: The threatened lynching of the Poe brothers at Winchester, Tennessee, took place at the end of March 1881, when about forty masked men set out at night for the jail holding John and Cicero Poe, who were accused of murder. Two townsmen met the party a mile from town and persuaded it to turn back, and no one was hurt. Wire reports on the brothers' conviction weeks later still recalled the "threatened lynching" that had "created so much excitement at Winchester."

The Poe brothers were charged with the murder of a man the papers called "young Baker." Some weeks before, they had been taken to Nashville "to prevent their being lynched," and on Monday, March 28, they were carried back to Winchester to stand trial. The Clarksville Weekly Chronicle reported "great fear of their being lynched" on their return.

According to a Winchester special relayed from Nashville at 1 a.m. on March 30, the brothers' arrival "revived the excitement that seemed to be dead." The special said that about forty masked men had been seen "last night" a mile from town on their way to the jail. Two citizens met them and persuaded them not to attack, after which "the mob dispersed and returned to their homes." The dispatch added that the jail was strongly guarded by men "determined to protect the prisoners."

No arrest of any of the masked men appears in the coverage. The Poes went to trial at Winchester in mid-April before Judge J. J. Williams, with a jury drawn from a panel of more than 200 and about forty witnesses. By then, the Morristown Gazette wrote, "no fear of lynching is now entertained."

On Saturday, April 16, the jury found both brothers guilty of murder in the first degree. On Monday a motion for a new trial was overruled, John Poe told the court they had not had a fair trial, and the judge sentenced both to hang on June 17, 1881. The case was appealed to the state Supreme Court, and Sheriff Turner took the prisoners to Nashville under guard, as fear was entertained "of their being lynched by the citizens, or rescued by their friends."

Only one full account of the night march survives in the coverage, a Nashville wire printed by the Omaha Daily Bee under the headline "WEAK-KNEED LYNCHERS." The wire garbled the brothers' names as "John and Giggo Poeyest," and a Wisconsin weekly, the Mineral Point Tribune, later ran a one-sentence version naming them as the Poe brothers. Tennessee papers followed the prisoners' return and trial, while the Nashville verdict wire, carried by the Chicago Daily Tribune and, as the "Poor brothers," by an Austin weekly, mentioned the threatened lynching only as a tag.

None of the reports gives the race of the Poes or of Baker, and none treats the episode in racial terms. The Winchester Home Journal's own trial report did not mention the March mob and judged that the prisoners had received "a fair and impartial trial."

accounts.gist: The Poes' arrival on Monday revived the excitement; about forty masked men heading for the jail were met a mile from town by two citizens who talked them out of attacking, and the jail was strongly guarded.

accounts.label: Tennessee state press
accounts.gist: The Poe brothers, earlier taken to Nashville to prevent their lynching, were brought back to Winchester for trial amid great fear that they would be lynched.

framing.detail: The Omaha Bee ran the Winchester special under the mocking headline 'WEAK-KNEED LYNCHERS,' while its text praised the guards 'determined to protect the prisoners.'
Later wire items mentioned the 'threatened lynching' only as a tag on the verdict news, without describing it.
